overview: This file combines a 1936 U.S. consular survey of newspaper coverage in Japanese-ruled Taiwan with a 1938 Department of State memorandum concerning restrictions on anthropological fieldwork there. The survey describes the prominence and changing character of American news in Taiwan newspapers, including reporting on Far Eastern policy, naval construction, trade, crime, elections and sports. The later memorandum summarizes the authorities’ refusal to permit Paul King Benedict to study relations between Taiwan’s governing and governed populations, recalls difficulties encountered by the Stewart Psycho-Ethnographic Expedition, and notes that expedition’s research among the Yami people of Orchid Island.

subfiles.title: News Survey of the Taihoku, Taiwan, Consular District
subfiles.to: Commercial Office, U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: The report assesses the amount and character of American news published in Taiwan newspapers during the preceding five years.
subfiles.summary: Maney explains that Taiwan newspapers devoted most nonlocal space to Japan but gave American news more attention than news from any other foreign country except China. Coverage emphasized U.S. policy in the Far East, naval construction and selected international crises, while internal American policy and relations with Latin America attracted little attention. Newspapers also published American stock quotations and reports from the Taiwan Trade Commissioner in New York about markets for camphor and tea; crime reporting had declined, but general interest in American construction, tariffs, elections and sports had increased. Copies were sent to the State Department’s Commercial Office, the Commercial Attaché in Tokyo and the Consulate General in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Paul King Benedict’s proposed anthropological studies
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes a Taihoku despatch reporting the colonial authorities’ refusal to permit Paul King Benedict to undertake independent anthropological research in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Benedict, a Harvard doctoral researcher, moved from Shanghai to Tamsui after war threatened to disrupt his work and applied for permission to conduct research in Taiwan. An official indicated that studies touching on relations between the governing and governed populations would not be tolerated and objected to Benedict’s description of Taiwan’s Chinese inhabitants as Chinese rather than Formosans and Japanese subjects. After permission was refused, Benedict left for Hong Kong. The memorandum also describes enclosed preliminary reports from the 1937 Stewart Psycho-Ethnographic Expedition concerning dream symbolism and the Yami people of Orchid Island, including an article by Nancy Grasby.

interest: The file offers two complementary views of information and knowledge production under Japanese colonial rule in Taiwan. The 1936 survey quantifies, at least impressionistically, the subjects through which Taiwanese readers encountered the United States, while the 1938 memorandum reveals official sensitivities surrounding ethnicity, colonial relations and foreign academic research. Its discussion of the Stewart expedition, the Yami and the several historical names for Orchid Island is particularly useful for historians of anthropology, colonial censorship and Indigenous Taiwan.
